episodes.title: First principles: What it takes to be a great product manager in the AI era | Sherif Mansour
episodes.description:
Sherif Mansour is Head of AI and Product Craft at Atlassian (the company behind Jira and Confluence), where he has spent 17 years building and scaling some of the most successful enterprise products in history. He joined Atlassian as its first PM on Confluence, eventually becoming its first Distinguished PM, and now leads both the craft of product management across the company and Atlassian’s AI product strategy.
We discuss:
1. Why a PM’s #1 job is to build a “shared brain”
2. The artist, the scientist, and the GM: three types of PM, and how to tell which one you are
3. Why PM roles are growing fastest in the AI era
4 Why Atlassian is hiring more juniors than ever
5. The most common mistake new PM managers make

2. Why Muse waited seven months to launch, despite getting started before most of its competitors
3. How Nat Friedman, Alex Wang, and Mark Zuckerberg each left their imprint on the product
4. How the team uses “agent swarms” to surface user insights at scale
5. The use case nobody on the team predicted
6. How Jolly, a placeholder avatar, became an icon
7. The two levers that actually move activation for an AI agent
8. The #1 thing Mona looks for in PMs today

episodes.title: How a 19-year-old intern built the growth engine behind this $2B AI company | Hector Serrano
episodes.description:
Hector Serrano runs one of the most innovative and successful paid growth programs in Silicon Valley. As Head of Content at Wispr Flow, a leading AI voice-to-text tool, he built a roster of 50 creators who drive 500 to 600 paid user-generated content (UGC) ads every month. The creators are paid a cut of ad spend, and the best of them earn over $13,000 a month. It’s a playbook the best DTC brands have used for years, now adapted for SaaS. Hector joined Wispr Flow at 19, before the product had PMF, and over the past year, Wispr Flow has grown revenue 30x and raised at a $2 billion valuation.
We discuss:
1. Why paid UGC is one of the biggest untapped growth levers right now
2. The step-by-step playbook for building a successful paid-UGC program
3. Why the best marketers are “allergic to AI”
4. What makes a great modern marketing hire
5. Why YouTube is the most underrated growth lever in SaaS
episodes.descriptionCN:
赫克托·塞拉诺 (Hector Serrano) 运营着硅谷最具创新性和最成功的付费成长计划之一。作为领先的 AI 语音转文本工具 Wispr Flow 的内容主管，他建立了一个由 50 名创作者组成的名单，每月推出 500 至 600 个付费用户生成内容 (UGC) 广告。创作者会从广告支出中获得一定比例的报酬，其中最好的人每月收入超过 13,000 美元。这是最好的 DTC 品牌多年来使用的剧本，现在适用于 SaaS。 Hector 于 19 岁时加入 Wispr Flow，当时该产品还没有 PMF，在过去的一年里，Wispr Flow 的收入增长了 30 倍，估值达到 20 亿美元。
我们讨论：
1. 为什么付费 UGC 是目前尚未开发的最大增长杠杆之一
2. 构建成功的付费 UGC 项目的分步指南
3. 为什么最好的营销人员“对人工智能过敏”
4. 是什么造就了优秀的现代营销人员
5. 为什么 YouTube 是 SaaS 领域最被低估的增长杠杆

episodes.title: An 86-minute guide to finding PMF | Rob Snyder (Author, The Power of Pull)
episodes.description:
Rob Snyder is the author of The Power of Pull and writes the newsletter The Physics of Startups. He has advised more than 50 startups on growing from zero to $1 million in ARR, drawing on his own experience as a founder who spent two years pushing a product the market didn’t want before accidentally stumbling onto what actually works. In this episode, we walk step by step through his framework for finding product-market fit, from coming up with an idea to closing your first handful of deals.
We discuss:
1. The PULL framework: Project, Unavoidable, List of options, Limitations
2. Where the best startup ideas come from
3. Tactics for cold outreach and running your first sales call
4. Why Rob advises against design partners
5. Goblin mode: what to do when nothing is working
6. How to apply the PULL framework inside larger companies
episodes.descriptionCN:
罗布·斯奈德 (Rob Snyder) 是《拉力的力量》一书的作者，也是时事通讯《初创公司的物理学》的作者。他利用自己作为创始人的经验，为 50 多家初创公司提供了从零到 100 万美元的 ARR 增长建议，他花了两年时间推出市场不想要的产品，然后意外地发现了真正有效的产品。在本集中，我们将逐步介绍他寻找产品与市场契合度的框架，从提出想法到完成第一笔交易。
我们讨论：
1. PULL 框架：项目、不可避免的问题、选项列表、限制
2. 最好的创业创意来自哪里
3. 冷外展和第一次销售拜访的策略
4. 为什么 Rob 不建议设计合作伙伴
5.妖精模式：什么都不起作用时该怎么办
6. 如何在大公司内部应用PULL框架

episodes.title: Inside the black box of AI: How AI models actually think | Emmanuel Ameisen (Anthropic)
episodes.description:
Emmanuel Ameisen is an interpretability researcher at Anthropic, where he looks inside LLMs like Claude to understand how they think. Before joining Anthropic, he spent years in applied ML at Stripe and Insight, and is the author of Building Machine Learning Powered Applications. His research has produced some of the most striking findings in the field: that models form general representations of concepts, plan many tokens ahead without stating those plans explicitly, and may exhibit something structurally similar to the distinction between conscious and unconscious processing in humans.
We discuss:
1. Why the “next-token predictor” framing undersells how models actually plan and think
2. Why anthropomorphizing AI can actually be the right approach
3. Why models are “grown,” not built
4. What the “J space” reveals about model self-awareness
5. The smooth scaling curve behind what look like sudden capability jumps
6. How interpretability connects to AI alignment and safety
episodes.descriptionCN:
Emmanuel Ameisen 是 Anthropic 的可解释性研究员，他深入研究像 Claude 这样的法学硕士，以了解他们的想法。在加入 Anthropic 之前，他在 Stripe 和 Insight 从事应用机器学习工作多年，并且是《构建机器学习驱动的应用程序》一书的作者。他的研究产生了该领域一些最引人注目的发现：模型形成概念的一般表示，提前计划许多标记而无需明确说明这些计划，并且可能在结构上表现出类似于人类有意识和无意识处理之间的区别的东西。
我们讨论：
1. 为什么“下一个令牌预测器”框架低估了模型实际计划和思考的方式
2. 为什么人工智能拟人化实际上是正确的方法
3. 为什么模型是“成长”的，而不是构建的
4.“J空间”揭示了模特的自我意识
5.看似突然的能力跳跃背后的平滑缩放曲线
6. 可解释性如何与人工智能一致性和安全性联系起来

episodes.title: Scaling Linear's GTM to $100M+ ARR — Cristina Cordova, COO
episodes.description:
Over half the issues created in Linear now come from agents instead of people.
I sat down with Cristina Cordova (COO at Linear) to talk about what that does to the software industry. They shipped an MCP server early, watched agents take over half the work, and then had to answer an uncomfortable question: if your product is mostly a database an agent writes to, why would humans open the app?
A few things I didn't expect. Three weeks into the job she stood up at an offsite and crossed "go enterprise" off the company goals, and they didn't go after enterprise until two years later. They've never hired a single SDR, and they don't do forward deployed engineering.
We also got into the AI budget every startup is tapping into and why she thinks it's already tightening, what it takes to cannibalize yourself before someone else does, and pricing on outcomes.

A camera moves around a person. Halfway around, the model has to draw the back of a head it has never seen. How much can it learn about that missing view just by watching video? That’s the question we put to Andreas Blattmann and Dustin Podell of Black Forest Labs.
Their answer runs through FLUX 3. BFL trained one backbone on images, video and audio. There’s personal history here. Stable Diffusion is why Dustin left his software job and why swyx started Latent Space. They revisit the first FLUX training run in a French chalet, the photo experiment behind FLUX Kontext, and some of the things people actually use these models for, from restoring old family photos to generating a clip with synchronized sound.
This episode is sponsored by Deepgram. Deepgram is the voice AI infrastructure behind natural conversation—bringing speech-to-text, text-to-speech, voice-focused LLMs, and agents to teams building with voice AI.

The Home Depot's founding story is like an Avengers movie… if the Avengers got fired, went broke, and stacked empty paint cans ten feet high to look legitimate. After being unceremoniously fired from their previous hardware chain at ages 48 and 35, Bernie Marcus and Arthur Blank took the words of their New York banker Ken Langone (who had also just accidentally caused their firings) to heart: they'd just been "kicked in the ass with a golden horseshoe.” They proceeded to author the greatest compounding story in American retail history, helped by some legendary cameos along the way from Sol Price, Jamie Dimon, and Ross Perot (to name a few). And the ending is as good as any superhero film: from its 1981 IPO to today, The Home Depot has been the single highest-returning equity in the entire US stock market — higher than Apple, Microsoft, Berkshire Hathaway, and everything else!

episodes.description:
In 1984, the Walt Disney Company was worth more dead than alive. Disney Animation — the heart of Walt's famous flywheel — had stagnated for years, bleeding away talent while corporate raiders circled, salivating over offers to sell off the film library to MGM and offload the parks to hotel operators. But what followed instead was the greatest turnaround in media history under Michael Eisner and Frank Wells. Beauty and the Beast. The Lion King. Broadway. Bringing the Disney Vault home on VHS and DVD. And the greatest media acquisition of all time — ESPN.
And then... it all almost fell apart. Again. Euro Disney turned into a money pit. Boardroom and executive infighting ran rampant. Animation descended into a dumpster fire. (Remember Chicken Little? Us neither.) Comcast — Comcast!! — tried to steal the company via a hostile takeover. Out of the chaos, a new generation of Disney management emerged under Bob Iger to stage yet another epic comeback with Pixar, Marvel and Lucasfilm, creating the defining media empire of the 21st century…until the tech companies came along. Tune in for the ultimate Acquired thrill ride: Disney, Part II.

episodes.title: AI Software Factories
episodes.description:
“Clearly there are 100x or 1,000x engineers now. The world hasn’t adjusted.”
— Guillermo Rauch (Vercel)
Guillermo: I’ve been really pilled with this idea of software factories. You used to ship the output directly, and everything inside the company was how good is person A at shipping output B? And now what’s happening is the way that I’m judging you as an engineer is, are you producing the factory that will produce multiplicative outputs B through Z, right?
We used to believe, and it used to be somewhat controversial, that there’s 10X engineers. Now clearly there’s 100X or 1,000X engineers. And the world hasn’t fully adjusted to this.
@naval: I used to get flamed on Twitter for saying there are 10X engineers, because it flies in the face of so much equality philosophy that everyone’s equal. But the reality is, when you’re operating in idea domains—when you’re operating in intellectual domains and virtual digital domains—it’s not even 10X. It’s 100X or 1,000X, and it always has been.
Satoshi, Notch, the guy who invented JavaScript, the Brendan Eichs of the world. John Carmack. These are 1,000X programmers.
Not to even mention if you choose the right thing to work on versus the wrong thing to work on, that’s an infinity difference. And it could just be not necessarily even a better programmer, just one who had a better judgment of what to work on in the first place.
And now obviously it’s less controversial, because of AI leverage.
episodes.descriptionCN:
“显然现在有 100 倍或 1,000 倍的工程师。世界还没有调整。”
— 吉列尔莫·劳赫 (Vercel)
Guillermo：我对软件工厂的想法非常着迷。你以前直接运送输出，公司内部的一切都是A在运送输出B时有多好？现在发生的事情是我对你作为一名工程师的评价，你是否正在生产将产生乘法输出 B 到 Z 的工厂，对吗？
我们曾经相信，有 10X 工程师的存在，但也曾经存在一些争议。现在显然有 100 倍或 1,000 倍的工程师。世界还没有完全适应这一点。
@naval：我曾经因为说有 10X 工程师而在 Twitter 上受到攻击，因为它违背了人人平等的平等理念。但现实是，当你在创意领域运作时——当你在知识领域和虚拟数字领域运作时——它甚至不是 10 倍。它是 100 倍或 1,000 倍，而且一直都是。
Satoshi，Notch，JavaScript 的发明者，世界上的 Brendan Eichs。约翰·卡马克.这些是 1000 倍的程序员。
更不用说你选择正确的工作还是错误的工作，这是一个无穷大的差异。而且不一定是更好的程序员，只是一个对首先要做什么有更好判断的人。
现在，由于人工智能的影响力，它的争议显然减少了。

episodes.title: 5 ways to get the most out of Gemini 4 Neon
episodes.description:
Gemini 4 Neon is LIVE, brining frontier-level intelligence with fast end-to-end task completion, try it for yourself:
In this solo episode, I break down Gemini 4 Neon, Google's new model, after testing it inside Antigravity. I start with builds from the community: motion design for a Pelican product, a robot dog on uneven limestone, and two pinball games with multiball physics,. Then I cover where to run Neon, five ways to get the most out of it, and five ways to make money or save time with it. I close with four honest caveats about brevity, writing habits, confusing naming, and Antigravity itself.
Key Points
• Neon handles physics, motion graphics, and 3D at a level that opens up games, hardware prototypes, and vibe manufacturing.
• The same model jumped from 12.8% to 39% on coding inside Antigravity, so I do my big builds there.
• High thinking is my sweet spot: 32% cheaper than Carbon, while extra high burns 70% more for under two points.
• /swarm spins up an AI team of researchers, designers, and engineers that can finish a big build overnight.
• Playable lead magnets and custom demos for prospects are two of the fastest ways I see to earn with Neon.
• Neon writes well once I ask for longer answers and tell it to drop em dashes and contrast clichés.
Numbered Section Summaries
1. Community Builds That Show the Range
Chetasula shared Neon's motion design for a Pelican product, and as someone who builds apps and hunts for mascots and motion design, I find it stunning. Another builder's piece got me thinking about hardware companies and prototypes, which ties back to my Argon episode on vibe manufacturing. Neon feels strong at this kind of hardware work.
2. Physics That Holds Up
One builder pushed Neon to add uneven limestone terrain to stress test robot dog biomechanics, and it added per-paw slope adaptation, five-point obstacle scanning, and spine torsion. It reminds me of the Boston Dynamics dogs, and I can picture whole games and worlds built this way. Next to GPT 6.2 Astra on the pelican-riding-a-bike test, Neon's physics feel like a different world.
3. Games and Apps From a Prompt
One builder made two pinball games with Blender and WebGPU, with generated play field art, PBR and stained glass maps, multiball physics, and procedural audio. They remind me of the Windows XP pinball game, and they're live with people playing them.
4. Five Ways to Get the Most Out of Neon
I set thinking to high, and I build inside Antigravity instead of the bare wrapper, which explains why people on X split so hard on this model. I use the orchestrator for daily work and /swarm for big builds, assigning a researcher, a front-end designer, a front-end engineer, and a back-end engineer before I go to sleep. I always give it a verification loop (open the browser, click buttons, fix bugs), and I put context first and demand facts, which triggers automatic caching and stops drift.
5. Lead Magnets and Trojan Horse Demos
Neon builds playable lead magnets, 3D configurators, and mini games that capture emails and get shared on X and Instagram, work agencies charge $10,000 to $100,000 for. For a Trojan horse demo, I paste in a business URL, like a Chick-fil-A in Toronto, let Neon scrape it, build that store a calculator or tool, and send it over. If I were 20 and chasing cash flow, I'd redesign stale websites and offer them for $50 or $100 a month.
6. Finance, Back Office, and Overnight Products
Neon is great with data: messy invoices go in, and a working financial model and audit come out. I ran my own company's numbers through it, and it feels like having a CFO-like partner. It also handles lead routing, CRM ops, and reconciliation for less than the competition, and with swarms, agent teams research, build, and QA micro products and directories while I ship.

Gemini 4 Neon 已上线，将前沿智能与快速的端到端任务完成相结合，亲自尝试一下：
在这一集中，我在 Antigravity 中测试了 Google 的新型号 Gemini 4 Neon 后对其进行了分解。我从社区的构建开始：Pelican 产品的运动设计、不平坦石灰岩上的机器狗以及两个具有多球物理原理的弹球游戏。然后我会介绍在哪里运行 Neon、充分利用它的五种方法，以及利用它赚钱或节省时间的五种方法。最后，我对简洁性、写作习惯、令人困惑的命名和反重力本身提出了四点诚实的警告。
要点
• Neon 在一定程度上处理物理、动态图形和 3D，从而开启了游戏、硬件原型和氛围制造。
• 同一模型在 Antigravity 内进行编码的比例从 12.8% 跃升至 39%，所以我在那里进行大型构建。
• 高思维是我的最佳选择：比碳便宜 32%，而超高燃烧量则多燃烧 70%，不到两点。
• /swarm 组建了一个由研究人员、设计师和工程师组成的人工智能团队，可以在一夜之间完成大型构建。
• 可玩的铅磁铁和针对潜在客户的定制演示是我认为通过 Neon 赚钱的两种最快方式。
• 当我要求更长的答案并告诉它去掉破折号并对比陈词滥调时，Neon 写得很好。
编号部分摘要
1.展示范围的社区建设
Chetasula 分享了 Neon 为 Pelican 产品设计的动作设计，作为一个构建应用程序并寻找吉祥物和动作设计的人，我发现它令人惊叹。另一篇建筑商的文章让我思考了硬件公司和原型，这与我关于氛围制造的 Argon 剧集有关。 Neon 对这种硬件工作感觉很强。
2. 物理原理成立
一位建筑商推动 Neon 添加不平坦的石灰岩地形，以对机器狗生物力学进行压力测试，并添加了每爪坡度适应、五点障碍物扫描和脊柱扭转功能。它让我想起了波士顿动力公司的狗，我可以想象以这种方式构建的整个游戏和世界。在鹈鹕骑自行车测试中，与 GPT 6.2 Astra 相比，Neon 的物理感觉就像是一个不同的世界。
3. 根据提示运行游戏和应用程序
一位构建者使用 Blender 和 WebGPU 制作了两款弹球游戏，其中包含生成的游戏场地艺术、PBR 和彩色玻璃地图、多球物理和程序音频。它们让我想起 Windows XP 的弹球游戏，而且它们就和人们一起玩。
4. 充分利用 Neon 的五种方法
我将思维定得很高，并且在反重力内部构建而不是裸露的包装，这解释了为什么 X 上的人们在这个模型上如此强烈地分裂。我使用 Orchestrator 进行日常工作，使用 /swarm 进行大型构建，在睡觉前分配一名研究员、一名前端设计师、一名前端工程师和一名后端工程师。我总是给它一个验证循环（打开浏览器，单击按钮，修复错误），并且我将上下文放在第一位并要求事实，这会触发自动缓存并停止漂移。
5. 磁铁和特洛伊木马演示
Neon 开发了可玩的铅磁铁、3D 配置器和迷你游戏，可以捕获电子邮件并在 X 和 Instagram 上分享，工作机构的收费为 10,000 至 100,000 美元。对于特洛伊木马演示，我粘贴一个企业 URL，例如多伦多的 Chick-fil-A，让 Neon 抓取它，构建一个存储计算器或工具的库，然后将其发送出去。如果我 20 岁并且追求现金流，我会重新设计过时的网站并以每月 50 或 100 美元的价格提供它们。
6. 金融、后台和隔夜产品
Neon 非常擅长处理数据：输入杂乱的发票，然后得出有效的财务模型和审计。我通过它运行了我自己公司的数据，感觉就像有一个类似首席财务官的合作伙伴。它还以低于竞争对手的价格处理潜在客户路由、CRM 操作和对账，并在我发货时与群体���代理团队研究、构建和 QA 微型产品和目录。

episodes.title: Robots vs Self Driving
episodes.description:
I sit down with Adrien Gaidon, Co-founder and Chief Strategy Officer of Walden Robotics, to map out where the openings sit in robotics and physical AI. Adrien explains how teams now teach robots with data, why deployment data carries the most value, and why Walden picked wheels and two-finger grippers for factory work. We dig into the opportunities around the big labs: data with scarce access, supply chain, teleoperation, insurance, software tools, and niche robots. If robotics feels like a game for companies with $300 million seed rounds, this episode lays out the smaller ways in too.
This episode was made possible thanks to Anthropic (the team behind Claude) for hosting us at Claude Founder house and sponsoring the episode.
Key Points
• Deployment data carries the most value, and teams earn it by putting robots on production floors.
• A strong data business sits where scarce access meets data that is useful for robots.
• Data, compute, and manufacturing are linked bottlenecks that a robotics company widens together.
• Robots that learn from deployment gain value over time, which opens new ways to price and sell them.
• Bundling many small tasks makes automation pay where each task alone falls short.
• Founders can pick their level of hard, from general-purpose robots to one-task niches like welding or gardening.
Numbered Section Summaries
1. From Programming to Teaching
Factory robots used to follow programmed points in space, blind to anything in their path. Adrien explains that teams now teach robots with data: web, video, and language data build a common-sense foundation model, and task demonstrations build the skill. 购买数据可以加快团队合作速度，但 Walden 最看重部署数据，而公司通过与丰田等制造商合作来获得这些数据。对于任何开始数据业务的人来说，阿德里安指出特权访问，例如家族企业、朋友或对咖啡等爱好的深入了解，再加上可以帮助机器人完成仍然难以完成的任务的数据。他用 Ikigai 扩展了维恩图，Ikigai 是一种日本理念，即找到你所爱的东西、世界需要的东西以及它所付出的代价。
3. 人类团队中的机器人
阿德里安称他的团队为“人类团队中的机器人专家”，并以瓦力和约翰尼五世为模型。 Walden 为其机器人设计了一个不对称的头部，因此它看起来很好奇，并调整其动作以使其感觉友好。公司名称源自梭罗的《瓦尔登湖》及其自力更生、简单和有目标的价值观。阿德里安预计 10 年内将出现数以百万计的机器人、制造业的繁荣、更便宜的基础设施项目以及像钢铁侠一样建造的人。
4.随着时间的推移而获得价值的机器人
较旧的机器人作为资本支出出售，并多年���重复相同的动作。会学习的机器人提供服务，而教会他们更多知识的客户可以获得更高的投资回报率，Adrien 将这与 Jensen Huang 的名言“买得越多，节省得越多”联系在一起。我指出从按席位和硬件定价转向按结果和按代币付费的转变，Adrien 鼓励创始人重新考虑客户想要如何购买。
5. 创始人可以从哪里开始
阿德里安列出了开放领域：数据、高混合和大批量生产的供应链、机器人公司销售和设计方面的工作、较慢机器人的远程操作以及机器人和振动制造产品的保险。软件创始人可以卖铲子，就像 Weights & Biases 所做的那样，Adrien 的团队是 OpenAI 之前的第一个客户。他建议创始人从 Russ 在 YouTube 上的讲座开始，然后在焊接、咖啡师机器人或园艺等领域寻找优势。

episodes.title: How to design an agent harness
episodes.description:
I sit down with Jon Noronha, co-founder and chief product officer of Gamma, to break down agent harnesses and the startup openings around them. Jon explains how Gamma rebuilt its product as a creative agent this year and walks me through the roughly 20 models and 200 calls behind one finished presentation. We talk about AI smell, why taste carries more weight than evals in creative work, how Gamma tests a new model within the hour, and the fast mode test that lost to good friction. Jon also shares the harnesses he wants to see, from a Slack agent that learns his voice to a couch shopping tool that checks the fit in your room. If you want to build a vertical agent, this episode gives you a clear model of what a harness is and where your edge can come from.
This episode was made possible thanks to Anthropic (the team behind Claude) for hosting us at Claude Founder house and sponsoring the episode.
Numbered Section Summaries
1. What is an Agent Harness
Gamma started in 2020, took off in 2023, and spent this year rebuilding its product from preset LLM workflows into an agent. Jon defines the harness as the tools an agent uses to act in its environment, inspect its own work, and ask the user for preferences, with Claude Code as the best-known example for programming. I call harnesses the new wrappers, and Jon agrees, since the wrapping is most of the work and even OpenAI and Anthropic put heavy effort into harness development.
2. Inside One Gamma Prompt
When someone pastes messy notes and asks for 20 slides, Gamma spins up a cloud sandbox, asks a few questions through a form, and pulls context from Notion, Slack, or Linear. It writes an outline, picks a template with vision models and embedding search, then generates text, layouts, images, and charts in parallel in about a minute. A vision model checks every slide for misaligned text, cropped heads, and weak contrast, and after rounds of fixes the deck has used about 20 models and 200 calls.
3. Where Vertical Harnesses Fit
Jon looks for problems that differ from coding: subjective work where people disagree on what good looks like and care about the specifics of the output. He likes personal video games for non-technical players and sees physical services, legal tech, and medical tech as active areas, though I'd pass on legal tech today because it feels crowded. Jon names three kinds of edge: a distinct vision you move toward faster, proprietary data, and businesses that mix AI with hardware or real-life services.
4. Image Models, Niches, and Loving the Work
Jon calls AI image models underhyped, since most people use them for menus and logos while Gamma uses about 10 image models for diagrams, textures, and icons. A couch shopping harness could render a couch in your room, measure it in pixels to tell a 58-inch from a 68-inch fit, and suggest a better option, with interior designers and pros at companies like Restoration Hardware as durable buyers. Jon closes with advice to pick work you could dogfood eight hours a day, and I add my rule to marry the niche and date the product.

我与 Gamma 联合创始人兼首席产品官乔恩·诺罗尼亚 (Jon Noronha) 坐下来，详细剖析了代理人的束缚以及围绕他们的初创企业空缺。 Jon 解释了 Gamma 今年如何作为创意代理重建其产品，并带我了解了一次完成的演示背后的大约 20 个模型和 200 个调用。我们谈论人工智能气味，为什么在创造性工作中味道比评估更重要，Gamma 如何在一小时内测试新模型，以及失去良好摩擦的快速模式测试。乔恩还分享了他想要看到的安全带，从学习他的声音的 Slack 代理到检查房间适合度的沙发购物工具。如果您想构建一个垂直代理，本集将为您提供一个清晰的模型，了解什么是安全带以及您的优势来自何处。
这一集的成功得益于 Anthropic（Claude 背后的团队）在 Claude 创始人之家接待我们并赞助了这一集。
编号部分摘要
1. 什么是代理安全带
Gamma 始于 2020 年，起飞于 2023 年，并在这一年将其产品从预设的 LLM 工作流程重建为代理。 Jon 将线束定义为代理用来在其环境中行动、检查其自身工作���询问用户偏好的工具，其中 Claude Code 是最著名的编程示例。我将线束称为新的包装器，Jon 同意，因为包装是大部分工作，甚至 OpenAI 和 Anthropic 都在线束开发上投入了大量精力。
2. 内部一个伽玛提示
当有人粘贴凌乱的笔记并要求提供 20 张幻灯片时，Gamma 会启动一个云沙箱，通过表单提出几个问题，并从 Notion、Slack 或 Linear 中提取上下文。它编写大纲，选择带有视觉模型和嵌入搜索的模板，然后在大约一分钟内并行生成文本、布局、图像和图表。视觉模型会检查每张幻灯片是否存在未对齐的文本、裁剪的头部和弱对比度，经过几轮修复后，该幻灯片已使用了大约 20 个模型和 200 个调用。
3. 垂直安全带适合的位置
乔恩寻找与编码不同的问题：主观工作，人们对好的外观有不同意见，并关心输出的细节。他喜欢非技术玩家的个人视频游戏，并将物理服务、法律技术和医疗技术视为活跃领域，尽管我今天不想谈法律技术，因为它感觉很拥挤。 Jon 列举了三种优势：朝着更快、专有数据迈进的独特愿景，以及将人工智能与硬件或现实服务相结合的业务。
4. 形象模型、利基市场和热爱工作
Jon 称 AI 图像模型被低估了，因为大多数人将它们用于菜单和徽标，而 Gamma 使用大约 10 个图像模型用于图表、纹理和图标。沙发购物安全带可以在你的房间里渲染一张沙发，以像素为单位进行测量，以区分 58 英寸和 68 英寸的尺寸，并提出更好的选择，室内设计师和 Restoration Hardware 等公司的专业人士都是持久的买家。乔恩最后建议选择每天八小时可以进行测试的工作，我添加了与利基市场结合并确定产品日期的规则。

episodes.description:
Gemini 4 Neon is LIVE, brining frontier-level intelligence with fast end-to-end task completion, try it for yourself:
In this solo episode, I break down Gemini 4 Neon, Google's new model, after testing it inside Antigravity. I start with builds from the community: motion design for a Pelican product, a robot dog on uneven limestone, and two pinball games with multiball physics,. Then I cover where to run Neon, five ways to get the most out of it, and five ways to make money or save time with it. I close with four honest caveats about brevity, writing habits, confusing naming, and Antigravity itself.
Timestamps

01:24 – Great Builds and Demos
06:26 – Where to run Neon
07:59 – Get the Most Out of Neon
09:55 – Ways to Make Money With Neon
13:13 – Honest Caveats
15:16 – Closing Thoughts
Key Points
• Neon handles physics, motion graphics, and 3D at a level that opens up games, hardware prototypes, and vibe manufacturing.
• The same model jumped from 12.8% to 39% on coding inside Antigravity, so I do my big builds there.
• High thinking is my sweet spot: 32% cheaper than Carbon, while extra high burns 70% more for under two points.
• /swarm spins up an AI team of researchers, designers, and engineers that can finish a big build overnight.
• Playable lead magnets and custom demos for prospects are two of the fastest ways I see to earn with Neon.
• Neon writes well once I ask for longer answers and tell it to drop em dashes and contrast clichés.
Numbered Section Summaries
1. Community Builds That Show the Range
Chetasula shared Neon's motion design for a Pelican product, and as someone who builds apps and hunts for mascots and motion design, I find it stunning. Another builder's piece got me thinking about hardware companies and prototypes, which ties back to my Argon episode on vibe manufacturing. Neon feels strong at this kind of hardware work.
2. Physics That Holds Up
One builder pushed Neon to add uneven limestone terrain to stress test robot dog biomechanics, and it added per-paw slope adaptation, five-point obstacle scanning, and spine torsion. It reminds me of the Boston Dynamics dogs, and I can picture whole games and worlds built this way. Next to GPT 6.2 Astra on the pelican-riding-a-bike test, Neon's physics feel like a different world.
3. Games and Apps From a Prompt
One builder made two pinball games with Blender and WebGPU, with generated play field art, PBR and stained glass maps, multiball physics, and procedural audio. They remind me of the Windows XP pinball game, and they're live with people playing them.
4. Five Ways to Get the Most Out of Neon
I set thinking to high, and I build inside Antigravity instead of the bare wrapper, which explains why people on X split so hard on this model. I use the orchestrator for daily work and /swarm for big builds, assigning a researcher, a front-end designer, a front-end engineer, and a back-end engineer before I go to sleep. I always give it a verification loop (open the browser, click buttons, fix bugs), and I put context first and demand facts, which triggers automatic caching and stops drift.
5. Lead Magnets and Trojan Horse Demos
Neon builds playable lead magnets, 3D configurators, and mini games that capture emails and get shared on X and Instagram, work agencies charge $10,000 to $100,000 for. For a Trojan horse demo, I paste in a business URL, like a Chick-fil-A in Toronto, let Neon scrape it, build that store a calculator or tool, and send it over. If I were 20 and chasing cash flow, I'd redesign stale websites and offer them for $50 or $100 a month.
6. Finance, Back Office, and Overnight Products
Neon is great with data: messy invoices go in, and a working financial model and audit come out. I ran my own company's numbers through it, and it feels like having a CFO-like partner. It also handles lead routing, CRM ops, and reconciliation for less than the competition, and with swarms, agent teams research, build, and QA micro products and directories while I ship.

5. 磁铁和特洛伊木马演示
Neon 开发了可玩的铅磁铁、3D 配置器和迷你游戏，可以捕获电子邮件并在 X 和 Instagram 上分享，工作机构的收费为 10,000 至 100,000 美元。对于特洛伊木马演示，我粘贴一个企业 URL，例如多伦多的 Chick-fil-A，让 Neon 抓取它，构建一个存储计算器或工具的库，然后将其发送出去。如果我 20 岁并且追求现金流，我会重新设计过时的网站并以每月 50 或 100 美元的价格提供它们。
